newsitem.title: UK: Dollar slips from highs to around 1.70 as mark up.
newsitem.headline: Dollar slips from highs to around 1.70 as mark up.

text.p: The dollar tripped off from its peaks against the mark in Europe to around 1.70 marks at midday as the German unit recovered composure. It clambered to one-month peaks against the lira.

Analysts said European investors were now seen returning to the mark after a brief hiatus and panic buying of the dollar following the clash between the German government and its central bank over plans to revalue its assets.
The mark was boosted against the lira, scoring one-month highs of 995.25 lire, after softer Italian GDP growth and rumours of Italian rating downgradings.
At 1120 GMT dollar/mark was trading at 1.6998/08 against 1.6992/02 in late Europe on Thursday. Dollar/yen stood at 116.30/6.40 against 116.14/24 in late Europe.

IBCA, the European credit rating agency, said it had no intention of changing the long-term local currency or the long-term foreign currency ratings of Italy's sovereign debt and the Italian treasury said other rating agencies also denied the report.
The mark recovered against the rest of its European crosses too, as initial fears of EMU being derailed - prompting investment into safe-havens like the dollar - were soothed, said analysts.

"If people think there is going to be an EMU (European Monetary Union) delay, they will move back into Bunds and the deutschmark will strengthen," said Sally Wilkinson, senior economist at Daiwa Europe.
Analysts said fears of a delay to EMU, slated to start in 1999, and mounting possibilities for a softer euro would help investment back into the mark.

But uncertainty in Europe over the outcome of French elections and Bonn's gold revaluation plan - which would help Germany cut back its deficits and make the grade for EMU - should continue to buoy safe-havens such as the dollar.

"There a lot of uncertainties concerning the gold and currency valuation plan of the Bundesbank...But we still have to wait for a vote in the lower house in Germany which intends to change the Bundesbank law," said Hans-Guenter Redeker, senior economist at Chase Investment Bank.

A vote against German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in the house, said Redeker, means the gold valuation deal could not be implemented. "This would raise a big question mark about Germany meeting the Maastricht criteria," he said.
Kohl, however, has the majority in Bonn to make the necessary changes to allow the revaluation.

But fundamentals clouding Europe could break, leading the mark higher. "In terms of economics the mark is likely to do fairly well, we are likely to see a shift in perceptions from an easing-rate bias in Europe, to a tightening rate bias," said James McKay, international economist at PaineWebber.
He said, however, a clear win for the opposition Socialists, who favour a flexible EMU interpretation, in French elections on Sunday would spook European markets.
"If the Socialists take an absolute majority - that would be detrimental to markets...We could see a delay or abandonment to the EMU project," said PaineWebber's MacKay.
"Then we would see a flight to quality assets such as dollar and mark," he added.
Against the yen, the dollar was also firm despite a senior official of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party saying he sees a chance of a credit tightening in Japan by early autumn.
"There is a chance of an interest rate increase by early autumn as economic fundamentals are getting better," Koji Omi, deputy chairman of the LDP's Policy Research Council said.
But poor industrial data for Japan, which showed industrial production fell 0.4 percent in April against forecasts for a 3.0 percent rise, has soothed expectations of higher rates.
"The recovery in Japan is not strong enough yet to warrant an interest-rate rise," said Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston, adding that U.S. data later on Friday should highlight the U.S. recovery.
US data later on Friday includes final first-quarter GDP and price index at 1230 GMT, the May Michigan business sentiment survey, Chicago PMI data and new home sales at 1400 GMT.
--Julia Meehan, London newsroom +4471 542 6701
